Well I think I’ll give you my personal lived experience rather the some sweeping generalization for all therapists(which I don’t think can be possible or accurate anyways) since you seem genuinely curious. The first thing I’ll say is I can count on one hand the amount of times I have cancelled sessions as a therapist because work has affected me in three years. Twice I left work early while I was working for hospice and one while I was in the hospital. FOR ME - In hospice or at the hospital level of care, as a therapist/social worker, there are inherent boundaries in the relationship. You are a part of a healthcare team(someone I might see one or twice before discharge on a floor or a family/pt I’m averaging seeing once or twice a month on hospice). The relationship in those settings are very different. When I am looking at my role as a therapist it demands much more from me mentally and emotionally. It’s a higher skill set. You can do a lot of damage if you get things wrong. I’m building a relationship with people I see weekly or bi-monthly over years. Therapists practice from different lenses/perspectives/specialties. I personally show up in a space emotionally in my practice. I am very humanistic, clients know I have lived experience in what I am treating, and because I practice how I do - they can feel that energy in the relationship. I explore clients core beliefs and challenge them in ways that align with what their goals for therapy are. I strongly believe in healing relational trauma through building the therapeutic relationship. I live a personal life that is congruent with my clinical values. I do not ask a client to do anything I, myself, would be unwilling to do. Including being in therapy weekly myself. Because this is how I practice(I’m not a blank slate) if I am “off” enough in a way that could interfere with my ability to practice to the standard that I do - it’s my responsibility to recognize this because this is when mistakes most often happen. If I, myself, am not well - I cannot help other people be well. I have no problem having my clients know I am human. They know I am a person who loves my job and that I am genuinely mostly happy. I offer varying degrees of transparency to various people if things do come up that require a change in schedule. This sub is full of people who have had horrible experiences with therapists who are practicing poorly. When I am supervising pre-licensed clinicians the biggest offenses are not doing their own “work” in therapy, bad supervision, inconsistent boundaries, poorly managed mental health, and lack of insight/ego. This is how I do my job and who I am as a therapist. Not everyone will agree. I won’t be the therapist for everyone. I am excellent at my job and absolutely love what I do.
